core: working definition of data integrity: accuracy and consistency of data over its lifetime (attributed to the standard Wikipedia formulation, with NIST's security dimension)
why integrity matters: decisions are only as good as the data (original wrong-price example in a product table)
the three classic types: entity integrity (rows uniquely identified), referential integrity (references point at real rows), domain integrity (values fit type and rules)
how databases enforce integrity: constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, foreign keys), each named with one line
integrity vs normalization: normalization prevents duplication; integrity enforces correctness

claims.claim: Data integrity is the maintenance of, and the assurance of, data accuracy and consistency over the data's entire life-cycle.
Data integrity also has a security dimension: it is the property that data has not been altered in an unauthorized manner, covering data in storage, during processing, and while in transit.
Entity integrity is the rule that every row in a table is uniquely identified, relying on unique keys so the same data is not listed multiple times.
Referential integrity is the rule that references between tables point at real rows; foreign key constraints maintain referential integrity and prevent orphaned records.
Domain integrity is the rule that values in a column fit the column's type, format, and allowed set of values.
A NOT NULL constraint ensures a column cannot hold a missing (NULL) value.
A UNIQUE constraint ensures all values in a column are distinct, and many UNIQUE constraints are allowed per table while only one primary key is allowed.
A CHECK constraint ensures values in a column satisfy a stated condition; when the condition evaluates to false, the entire insert or update is aborted and an error is raised.

Data types alone are too coarse to protect domain integrity: a price column should only accept positive values, but no standard data type enforces that, so a CHECK constraint is added on top of the type.

Decisions built on data are only as good as the data: a wrong price in a product table distorts checkout totals, reports, and business decisions, so integrity is a critical aspect of any system that stores, processes, or retrieves data.
Integrity rules are the database's immune system: constraints reject values that break declared rules before they are stored, but they cannot catch well-formed values that are factually wrong.
Normalization prevents duplication while integrity enforces correctness; the two are complementary rather than the same process.

positions: Wikipedia and IBM frame data integrity as the maintenance of and assurance of data accuracy and consistency over the data's lifetime (the quality view).
NIST's glossary defines data integrity as the property that data has not been altered in an unauthorized manner, in storage, during processing, and in transit (the security view).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson leads with the standard working definition (accuracy and consistency over the lifetime, attributed to Wikipedia's article) and presents NIST's framing as a complementary security dimension rather than a competing definition.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Relationship between data types and integrity.
positions: Data types restrict what kind of value a column can hold, which is part of domain integrity.
PostgreSQL notes the type-level restriction is too coarse for rules such as 'price must be positive', so additional constraints are needed.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats data types as the first layer of domain rules and constraints as the rules beyond type, and references the data-types topic as a sibling rather than teaching types here.
